target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers and give many workers time to vote
objection: A federal/national holiday does not require private employers to close or provide paid time off, and many low-income retail and service workers would still be on the job, so the holiday would not reliably give many working voters time away to vote.

target: AG1’s implication that a national holiday would benefit low-income workers
objection: Because low-income workers are concentrated in jobs that often continue operating on federal holidays, the holiday would leave their scheduling barriers largely in place and would therefore disadvantage them rather than reliably help them vote.

target: AG1’s claim that an Election Day holiday would substantially increase turnout
objection: Research and comparative evidence indicate that an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with other voting-access reforms, so the holiday is unlikely to produce substantial turnout gains on its own.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday is the right reform instead of other options
objection: State laws requiring employer time off for voting, or automatic voter registration, are more direct and reliable ways to improve voting access than a national holiday.

target: AG2’s objection that a federal holiday would not reliably give workers time off to vote
objection: A national holiday would, in practice, cause many schools and public offices to close and would often lead workplaces to reduce operations or offer flexibility, so it would create real time windows for many voters even without a mandate on every private employer.

target: AG2’s claim that low-income workers would be disadvantaged because holiday status would not help them
objection: That objection assumes low-income workers would still be unable to get meaningful time to vote on a holiday, but a national holiday is a universal calendar change that also increases holiday-related availability of schools and public services many low-income voters rely on, so it is not inherently disadvantageous to them.

target: AG2’s argument that other reforms make a holiday unnecessary
objection: Even if other voting-access reforms are also useful, that does not negate the value of removing a direct scheduling barrier; a holiday can still be justified as one part of improving turnout.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday does not produce a turnout solution
objection: A policy can be worth adopting because it promotes civic participation and democratic legitimacy even if it does not solve every voting-access problem by itself, so the fact that a holiday is not a complete solution is not a reason to reject it.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday would not reliably help parents because school closures are uncertain
objection: For many working parents, especially low-income parents, school-day supervision and childcare are a real barrier to voting, and a holiday would reduce that barrier by causing schools to close or shift schedules.

target: AG1’s claim that school closures on Election Day would reliably reduce childcare barriers for parents
objection: A federal holiday does not legally require all schools to close or change schedules, since many school closures depend on local policy; therefore childcare and supervision constraints would not be reliably reduced for all or even most parents.

target: AG1’s claim that low-income working families would especially benefit from school closures
objection: Low-income families depend heavily on school-based supervision and cannot count on schools to close or change schedules everywhere, so a national holiday would not provide them a dependable childcare/supervision improvement.

target: AG1’s assumption that school closure is enough to improve voting access
objection: If the holiday does not reliably reduce childcare and supervision constraints, then the main mechanism used to justify the holiday cannot be relied on to increase voting access for the groups most likely to face those barriers.

target: AG2’s claim that school closures are not reliable because local schools may not all close
objection: In practice, when a day is designated a federal holiday, school calendars commonly adjust so that many public and private schools close or run non-instructional schedules, making reduced supervision and childcare constraints predictable for most parents.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday status would reduce work-related barriers for low-income parents
objection: A national holiday does not require private employers to provide paid time off, and low-income workers are concentrated in jobs that often continue operating on federal holidays, so many would still be working during voting hours and unable to take time off safely.

target: AG1’s assumption that reduced childcare constraints translate into voting access
objection: Even if childcare needs are reduced, work schedules can still prevent voting during Election Day hours, so the childcare mechanism does not reliably create access for low-income working parents.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would reliably improve access for low-income working families
objection: Because low-income parents may still be unable to leave work, the holiday does not reliably improve access through the childcare mechanism and would leave the key work-time barrier in place.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday meaningfully removes work-time barriers for low-income workers
objection: Without legally guaranteed paid time off or wage protection, many low-income workers cannot afford or safely take time away from work, so the holiday would not reliably create the time they need to vote.

target: AG1’s claim that reduced childcare plus a holiday meaningfully helps low-income parents
objection: If low-income workers cannot afford or safely take unpaid or risky time off, then reductions in childcare or school constraints do not translate into reliable voting access.

target: AG1’s reliance on a holiday as the main reform
objection: More direct reforms—such as mandated employer accommodations or automatic voter registration—are better because a holiday alone leaves the work-time barrier uneven and non-guaranteed for low-income workers.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday predictably reduces schedule conflicts for working parents
objection: Although holidays often reduce school and workplace conflicts in practice, the policy still leaves many low-income workers without guaranteed time away, so it is not a dependable solution for them.

target: AG2’s claim that low-income workers would still lack reliable time off even with a holiday
objection: Absentee/mail voting means that lack of time away during Election Day hours does not necessarily prevent voting, and a holiday can help people complete and submit those ballots at home.

target: AG1’s absentee/mail voting argument
objection: Low-income workers often still lack free time around Election Day, and holiday timing can make mail or drop-off submission harder because mail services and drop-off locations may have reduced hours or slower processing, so they still may not have a workable opportunity to return absentee ballots.

target: AG2’s inference that a U.S. Election Day holiday would still leave many low-income workers without reliable voting time because employers need not close
objection: Many OECD democracies hold elections on weekends or holidays despite having large private-sector labor forces with low-income hourly workers, showing that holiday election days can still be compatible with workable voting time for those workers.

target: AG2’s reliance on the fact that U.S. holiday status does not force all employers to close
objection: International precedent suggests that the absence of a universal legal closure or paid-time-off requirement does not automatically mean low-income voters will lack reliable time to vote on a holiday election day.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday would likely leave many low-income workers without reliable time to vote
objection: Given OECD precedent for weekend/holiday elections, the inference that low-income workers would likely lack reliable voting time is not supported.
